<p class="lx-eyebrow">Eight components, the discipline behind each, and what system models borrow</p><div class="x1-fb"><details class="x1-fbd"><summary><b>Inverter</b> · Power electronics</summary><dl class="x1-dl"><dt>Asks</dt><dd><ul><li>How does it turn the direct current of solar panels and batteries into alternating current?</li><li>How fast can it respond, and does it hold on through a voltage dip?</li></ul></dd><dt>Models borrow</dt><dd>Its AC rating, its conversion losses, how fast it can change output and, in A17, whether it forms or follows the grid.</dd><dt>In this course</dt><dd><ul><li><b>DC to AC</b> (what it does): Solar cells make direct current; an inverter turns it into the grid's alternating current.</li></ul></dd><dt>Read next</dt><dd>Erickson and Maksimović, Fundamentals of Power Electronics (Springer)</dd></dl></details><details class="x1-fbd"><summary><b>Protective relay</b> · Power system protection</summary><dl class="x1-dl"><dt>Asks</dt><dd><ul><li>Which <span class="lx-term" data-term="circuit-breaker">breaker</span> should open, and how fast, when a line has a <span class="lx-term" data-term="fault">fault</span>?</li><li>How are its settings chosen so that healthy lines stay in service?</li></ul></dd><dt>Models borrow</dt><dd>Not the relay settings: equipment ratings, such as a line's thermal rating, and how often equipment is forced out of service.</dd><dt>In this course</dt><dd><ul><li><b>Thermal rating</b> (a line's limit): The most current a line or transformer can carry before it overheats; models keep flows under it. A relay is different: it detects a <span class="lx-term" data-term="fault">fault</span> and tells a breaker to open.</li></ul></dd><dt>Read next</dt><dd>Horowitz and Phadke, Power System Relaying (Wiley)</dd></dl></details><details class="x1-fbd"><summary><b>Turbine blade</b> · Aerodynamics and structural engineering</summary><dl class="x1-dl"><dt>Asks</dt><dd><ul><li>How much of the wind's power can the rotor catch?</li><li>Will the blade survive repeated gusts over its intended life?</li></ul></dd><dt>Models borrow</dt><dd>A power curve with its rated power, and how often the turbines are available.</dd><dt>In this course</dt><dd><ul><li><b>59.3%</b> (the Betz limit): The most of the wind's power any rotor can take, the Betz limit (physics).</li><li><b>0.52</b> (best measured power coefficient): The best measured <span class="lx-term" data-term="power-coefficient">power coefficient</span> of DOE's 1.5 MW test turbine: the share of the wind's power it turned into electricity.</li></ul></dd><dt>Read next</dt><dd>Burton, Jenkins, Sharpe and Bossanyi, Wind Energy Handbook (Wiley)</dd></dl></details><details class="x1-fbd"><summary><b>Gas-turbine combustor</b> · Combustion and thermodynamics</summary><dl class="x1-dl"><dt>Asks</dt><dd><ul><li>How hot can the flame burn before metal or emission limits are reached?</li><li>How low can the turbine run and still burn steadily?</li></ul></dd><dt>Models borrow</dt><dd>A heat rate, a ramp limit, a minimum load and a start time.</dd><dt>In this course</dt><dd><ul><li><b>7,535 Btu/kWh</b> (full-load tested heat rate, 2025): EIA's 2025 average full-load tested heat rate for U.S. natural-gas combined-cycle plants: 3,412 ÷ 7,535 = 45.3% of the fuel's energy becomes electricity at full load.</li><li><b>40 MW per hour</b> (ramp limit, Prairie Town): The ramp limit of Prairie Town's combined-cycle plant (illustrative).</li></ul></dd><dt>Read next</dt><dd>Turns, An Introduction to Combustion (McGraw-Hill)</dd></dl></details><details class="x1-fbd"><summary><b>Reactor core</b> · Reactor physics, thermal hydraulics and nuclear materials</summary><dl class="x1-dl"><dt>Asks</dt><dd><ul><li>How does the core hold its chain reaction steady?</li><li>How is heat carried away so that the fuel and the metal tubes that hold it stay within their limits?</li></ul></dd><dt>Models borrow</dt><dd>A thermal and an electric rating, an outlet temperature and a heat rate.</dd><dt>In this course</dt><dd><ul><li><b>about 300 °C</b> (outlet temperature): The outlet temperature of large water-cooled reactors.</li><li><b>10,443 Btu/kWh</b> (fleet heat rate, 2025): The U.S. nuclear fleet's 2025 heat rate: 3,412 ÷ 10,443 = 32.7% of the heat becomes electricity.</li></ul></dd><dt>Read next</dt><dd>Lamarsh and Baratta, Introduction to Nuclear Engineering (Pearson)</dd></dl></details><details class="x1-fbd"><summary><b>Electrolyzer stack</b> · Electrochemistry, catalysis and materials</summary><dl class="x1-dl"><dt>Asks</dt><dd><ul><li>How much electricity does a kilogram of hydrogen take?</li><li>How fast do the cells wear, and how low can the stack run?</li></ul></dd><dt>Models borrow</dt><dd>Electricity per kilogram of hydrogen for the whole system (stack, power supply, pumps and dryers), a minimum load and a stack life.</dd><dt>In this course</dt><dd><ul><li><b>57 kWh/kg</b> (whole-system electricity use): A16 assumes about 57 kWh per kilogram of hydrogen for the complete PEM electrolyzer system; stack design helps set that system value.</li><li><b>PEM 5%, alkaline 15%</b> (minimum loads): The lowest steady load of <span class="lx-term" data-term="pem-electrolyzer">PEM</span> and of <span class="lx-term" data-term="alkaline-electrolyzer">alkaline</span> electrolyzers, as a share of their size.</li></ul></dd><dt>Read next</dt><dd>U.S. Department of Energy, Hydrogen and Fuel Cell Technologies Office, Hydrogen Production: Electrolysis (energy.gov)</dd></dl></details><details class="x1-fbd"><summary><b>Battery cell</b> · Electrochemistry and materials science</summary><dl class="x1-dl"><dt>Asks</dt><dd><ul><li>How much energy does a cell hold, and how fast can it charge?</li><li>How do heat and cycling age it?</li></ul></dd><dt>Models borrow</dt><dd>A round-trip efficiency for the whole battery system, a duration (energy over power) and a life.</dd><dt>In this course</dt><dd><ul><li><b>85%</b> (round trip of the battery system): The course assumes 85% of the electricity sent into its utility-scale battery system comes back out: charging and discharging losses together, for the whole system, not one cell.</li><li><b>15 years</b> (life): The life the course gives that battery system.</li></ul></dd><dt>Read next</dt><dd>Linden's Handbook of Batteries (McGraw-Hill)</dd></dl></details><details class="x1-fbd"><summary><b>Control room</b> · Control engineering, operations and cybersecurity</summary><dl class="x1-dl"><dt>Asks</dt><dd><ul><li>How do operators see the grid every few seconds and send each plant its target output?</li><li>How are those systems kept safe from cyberattack?</li></ul></dd><dt>Models borrow</dt><dd>Operating rules: how often dispatch runs, how much reserve is held and which limits are watched.</dd><dt>In this course</dt><dd><ul><li><b>CIP</b> (cybersecurity standards): The mandatory Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP) standards of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) cover the bulk power system's cyber systems, in general not those on the distribution grid.</li></ul></dd><dt>Read next</dt><dd>Wood, Wollenberg and Sheblé, Power Generation, Operation, and Control (Wiley)</dd></dl></details></div><p class="lx-eyebrow" style="margin-top:10px">The kinds of number a model borrows</p><ul><li><b>Rating</b>: How much it can make, carry or store: MW, MWh, a line's limit.</li><li><b>Efficiency</b>: How much of what goes in comes out: a heat rate, a round trip, kWh per kilogram.</li><li><b>Ramp limit</b>: How fast its output can change, in MW per hour.</li><li><b>Minimum load</b>: The lowest output it can hold steadily, as a share of its size; below that it must stop.</li><li><b>Outlet temperature</b>: How hot the heat it gives is, which sets the uses that heat can serve.</li><li><b>Reliability and life</b>: Three separate numbers: how often it fails, how long each outage lasts, and how many years it serves before replacement.</li><li><b>Operating rule</b>: How the people and software running the grid decide: time steps, reserves, limits.</li></ul><p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you tap each component, sort what models borrow, and light the components by the kind of number they supply.</p>

<dl class="lx-ideas"><dt>Disciplines</dt><dd>Power electronics, protection, aerodynamics, combustion, reactor physics, electrochemistry and control each design a part of the system.</dd><dt>What crosses over</dt><dd>A system model borrows ratings, efficiencies, ramp limits, minimum loads, outlet temperatures, and reliability and life, plus the control room's operating rules.</dd><dt>What stays</dt><dd>Designs, materials and calculations stay with each discipline; the model sees them only through the numbers they lead to.</dd><dt>Cybersecurity</dt><dd>NERC's mandatory standards protect the bulk power system's cyber systems; distribution-grid devices are in general outside them.</dd></dl>
<!-- x01-ideas:end -->
</div>
</div>
<!-- x01-stop:start (written from the data by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-card xs-stop" id="x01-stop"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Where we stop</p><h3>This side topic stops at the nameplate</h3><p class="xs-stop-lede">Devices enter the course only as numbers: ratings, efficiencies, ramp limits and minimum loads, outlet temperatures, failure rates and lifetimes. Designing them belongs to each discipline.</p><div class="xs-stop-cols"><div><h4 class="xs-h">This side topic covers</h4><ul><li>What each discipline designs and which questions it answers.</li><li>Which numbers a system model borrows from it, and where this course uses them.</li><li>Where cybersecurity sits: standards for the bulk power system's control systems.</li></ul></div><div><h4 class="xs-h">Left to specialists</h4><ul><li>Design methods, physics and calculations for any device.</li><li>Testing, certification and equipment standards.</li><li>Running or securing a control room.</li></ul></div></div><h4 class="xs-h">Read next, three rungs</h4><ol class="xs-ladder"><li><b>Start here.</b> A short tour of turbines, generators and inverters, and how each makes electricity. <span class="xs-src"><a href="https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/how-electricity-is-generated.php">EIA, Electricity explained: How electricity is generated</a>, read 3 November 2026</span></li><li><b>Go further.</b> Pick one discipline and read its textbook: each component card above names one, in any recent edition. <span class="xs-src">The reading line on each component card, list of 7 November 2026</span></li><li><b>Go deep.</b> For control systems: how the mandatory cybersecurity standards reach the bulk power system, and where distributed resources stand. <span class="xs-src"><a href="https://nerc.com/globalassets/our-work/reports/white-papers/white_paper_cybersecurity_for-ders_and_der_aggregators.pdf">NERC, Cyber Security for Distributed Energy Resources and DER Aggregators (white paper)</a>, December 2022</span></li></ol></div>

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Where each borrowed number enters a model</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li><b>Efficiency.</b> A heat rate times a fuel price becomes a running cost per MWh in a dispatch model (<a href="m01-dispatch-to-lmp.html">M1</a>).</li>
<li><b>Ramp limit.</b> It becomes a rule linking one hour's output to the next (<a href="m02-unit-commitment.html">M2</a>).</li>
<li><b>Minimum load.</b> It becomes a lower bound on output while a unit runs, paired with an on or off choice (<a href="m02-unit-commitment.html">M2</a>).</li>
<li><b>Round trip.</b> It becomes the loss in a storage balance, hour by hour (<a href="m04-storage-multienergy.html">M4</a>).</li>
<li><b>Reliability.</b> A <span class="lx-term" data-term="forced-outage-rate">forced outage rate</span>, the share of time a unit is unexpectedly out, becomes the chance it is unavailable in each hour an adequacy simulation draws (<a href="a05-adequacy.html">A5</a>).</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
